newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan warns flag row could sink HK ties.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan warns flag row could sink HK ties.

text.p: Taipei on Tuesday warned of painful consequences if no deal was reached with rival China over Taiwan's crucial shipping links with Hong Kong after the British colony reverts to Chinese rule in July.
One of Taiwan's leading China policymakers said service could grind to a halt in a row over what flags ships should fly when plying routes between Taiwan and Hong Kong.

Kao Koong-lian said Taipei had no problem welcoming ships flying the red five-starred flag of the communist People's Republic of China (PRC) -- but only if Beijing and Hong Kong tolerated vessels that flew the flag of the exiled Republic of China (ROC) on Taiwan.
"We are not sensitive to have the vessels flying the PRC flag come into the ports of Taiwan," Kao, vice-chairman of the cabinet's Mainland Affairs Council, said in an interview.
"But they are the one who denies (ships flying) the ROC flag to go into the harbours of their ports," Kao told Reuters. "The problem is on their side."

Just 77 days before Hong Kong's July 1 absorption by China, Taipei and Beijing remain at loggerheads over whether Taiwan and Hong Kong-registered ships can hoist their flags when entering each other's waters.

China regards Taiwan as a renegade province and refuses to recognise the Republic of China, which has ruled the Nationalist redoubt since losing the mainland in a civil war in 1949 and fleeing to the island.
Likewise, Taipei refuses to recognise the People's Republic but has resisted popular calls to declare a sovereign Republic of Taiwan, fearing a military assault from the mainland.
Hong Kong's looming handover puts it at the centre of the two Chinas' historic rivalry.

Hong Kong is the channel through which more than US$30 billion in Taiwan investments have poured into China since the late 1980s, when a political thaw unleashed an explosion of unofficial Taiwan-China ties.

Hong Kong's post-handover constitution states that after July 1, Hong Kong-registered ships on international routes must fly communist China's flag along with its own Hong Kong Special Administrative Region flag.
Kao said he remained hopeful a mutually acceptable agreement would be worked out in April if Beijing showed good faith and recognised its own economic self-interest.

"If they (Beijing) are pragmatic, I think we can reach an arrangement or agreement by the end of this month," Kao said. "It's for the benefit of both Taiwan and Hong Kong and, indirectly, for the mainland side."
Taipei has authorised the semi-official Straits Exchange Foundation to negotiate with the Beijing-appointed Hong Kong Shipowners' Association, but no date or venue has been set.

Though companies believe there is a tacit agreement for business as usual after July 1, Kao warned that the absence of a deal ironing out the technical details could force a halt in Taiwan-Hong Kong shipping -- to everyone's disadvantage.
"If they don't allow our ships to go into Hong Kong harbour, then in the reciprocal way we will also not allow vessels from Hong Kong to come to the ports of Taiwan," Kao said.
"If this happened, it would hurt shipping companies of both Taiwan and Hong Kong...and the economy," he said. "We are not willing to see this kind of situation develop."

To avoid the sensitive sovereignty issue, Kao said Taiwan negotiators would propose that Taiwan and Hong Kong ships lower all flags and identify themselves through telex communications before entering each other's waters.

Taiwan, which still bans direct links with mainland China, said on Friday it would allow four shipping firms from China to sail directly across the Taiwan Strait -- cautiously easing a ban dating to their civil war split in 1949.
Taipei does not regard the service as direct shipping but rather as "offshore transshipment" because mainland cargoes will not be allowed to enter Taiwan customs.
Kao said Taipei could not allow true direct Taiwan-China links before Beijing recognised that the Republic of China still existed, if only on Taiwan and a few Taiwan-held islets.
Asked to describe the current Taipei-Beijing relationship, Kao said with a laugh: "It's cool...but it's picking up."
